messages.content: I want to recover relightable geometry and materials from three images taken under unknown illumination, while quantifying ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and lighting. How should I understand that goal?

It has two connected parts. The reconstruction should yield geometry and materials that can be used for relighting, rather than only an appearance that matches the three input images. At the same time, it should represent how uncertain the interpretation is: an observed appearance may not uniquely determine which aspects come from shape, which come from reflectance, and which come from illumination. The goal does not assume those ambiguities disappear.
So a visually plausible reconstruction of the three images would not, by itself, cover everything I asked for?

Right. Plausibility in the input images is not the entire objective. “Relightable” matters because the recovered geometry and materials are intended to account for appearance under other lighting as well. And quantifying ambiguity matters because a single plausible interpretation does not say how strongly the three images constrain shape, reflectance, and lighting.
Does “unknown illumination” mean lighting is one of the things that could be confused with the geometry and materials?

Yes. Illumination is not given for the three input images, so the interpretation has to account for lighting alongside geometry and materials. Conceptually, a change attributed to surface shape or reflectance might instead be partly attributed to lighting, or vice versa. That is the shape–reflectance–lighting ambiguity the goal asks to quantify; it does not prescribe a particular way to quantify it.
When I say materials here, is reflectance part of the same discussion?

Yes. Reflectance is the aspect of material appearance relevant to how the recovered scene responds to illumination. The goal names geometry and materials as the things to recover, and shape, reflectance, and lighting as the factors whose ambiguity should be quantified. Those formulations are compatible without implying that every material property can be uniquely recovered.
What are the concrete performance requirements?

There are two. First, reduce held-out relighting LPIPS by 15% versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. Second, achieve 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. The first concerns relighting quality under an LPIPS comparison; the second concerns whether the predictive intervals cover held-out intensity values at the specified rate.
Is the 15% an absolute change in LPIPS, or a comparison with that renderer?

It is a 15% reduction relative to the matched point-estimate inverse renderer’s held-out relighting LPIPS, not a reduction of 15 LPIPS units or 15 percentage points. For a purely arithmetic illustration, if that baseline’s LPIPS were 0.20, a 15% reduction would mean 0.17. That example is not a reported result or an assumed baseline value.
And what does “matched point-estimate inverse renderer” establish in that sentence?

It identifies the comparison baseline: a matched inverse renderer that gives a point estimate. The requirement specifies the LPIPS improvement relative to that baseline. It does not state exactly how the renderers are matched, so there is no need to infer particular model components, training arrangements, or experimental conditions from that word alone.
Why specify held-out relighting for LPIPS instead of just checking how well the three images are reproduced?

Because the stated requirement is about relighting beyond the images used as input. Reproducing those three images and obtaining low LPIPS on held-out relighting are distinct evaluations. The latter speaks more directly to the requested relightable geometry and materials, without by itself proving that every recovered property is uniquely identified.
I also want to be precise about the intervals. What makes a predictive interval nominally 90%?

“Nominal 90%” describes the coverage level the predictive intervals are intended to represent. The separate 85–95% requirement is about their observed coverage on held-out relighting intensities: what fraction of those intensity values fall inside their corresponding intervals. The allowed range is centered around 90%, but it does not demand exactly 90% observed coverage.
Would 90% coverage mean that 90% of the recovered geometry is correct?

No. The specified coverage applies to predictive intervals for held-out relighting intensities, not directly to geometry, material parameters, or a probability that an entire reconstruction is correct. Geometry, reflectance, and lighting are central to the ambiguity being quantified, but the numerical coverage target is stated specifically for intensity predictions.
Could you give me a simple way to read the 85–95% band without implying we have results already?

As a hypothetical illustration, if there were 100 held-out relighting intensity values, coverage within the target band would mean that 85 through 95 of those values fell within their corresponding nominal 90% predictive intervals. That only explains the percentage; it does not say how many values will be evaluated or what coverage will actually be achieved.
If intervals were extremely wide, could they cover many intensities without making the relighting accurate?

Coverage alone does not express everything about predictive usefulness or visual accuracy. That is one reason to keep the two stated requirements distinct: the held-out relighting LPIPS comparison addresses one aspect of output quality, while interval coverage addresses whether held-out intensities fall within the stated uncertainty ranges. The goal specifies those two tests, but it does not add a separate numerical interval-width requirement.
Conversely, would a good LPIPS score tell us the shape–reflectance–lighting ambiguity has been quantified?

Not on its own. LPIPS assesses the held-out relighting comparison in the first requirement. Quantifying ambiguity is an additional part of the goal, and the predictive-interval coverage requirement supplies a particular check on uncertainty in held-out relighting intensities. Neither a single quality score nor a single reconstructed shape automatically communicates every ambiguity among shape, reflectance, and lighting.
Am I being asked to pick one definitive explanation of each input image?

The wording asks for recovered relightable geometry and materials while quantifying ambiguity, so it should not be read as a claim that one explanation is definitively established by the three images under unknown illumination. It leaves open how a reconstruction and its uncertainty are represented. What must remain explicit is that shape, reflectance, and lighting can be difficult to disentangle.
Does the 85–95% requirement apply to every separate kind of surface or lighting condition?

No such subdivision is specified. The requirement, as stated, is 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. It would go beyond that wording to assert a separate coverage target for particular surfaces, lighting conditions, individual images, or material categories.
Then the main distinction is between recovering something usable for relighting and being honest about what the three images cannot pin down?

Yes. The goal combines those aims rather than treating uncertainty as a substitute for relighting quality, or relighting quality as proof of an unambiguous reconstruction. Its explicit numerical checks are a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer and 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities.

For the three-image reconstruction goal, I propose fitting a gauge-normalized mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior with diffusion priors, selecting LPIPS-medoid relightings, and conformally calibrating intensity intervals. Can we unpack what each part contributes?

Yes. The mesh, BRDF, and lighting describe the shape, reflectance, and illumination involved in producing the images. Fitting a posterior means retaining uncertainty over those quantities rather than committing only to one joint estimate. Gauge normalization addresses representational freedoms that could make equivalent descriptions look different; diffusion priors provide prior structure. LPIPS-medoid selection then chooses representative relighting outputs, while conformal calibration addresses the coverage of predictive intervals for relighting intensities. This is a proposed approach, not a claim that either performance target has been achieved.
Why call it a mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior instead of just a posterior over the reconstructed object?

Naming all three components makes the intended ambiguity explicit. A mesh describes geometry, a BRDF describes how a material reflects light, and lighting describes illumination. If uncertainty were discussed only as uncertainty about “the object,” it might obscure that different combinations of shape, reflectance, and lighting can explain the same visual evidence. A joint posterior provides a way to express those combinations without asserting that the three input images uniquely distinguish them.
Is gauge normalization meant to remove the ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and lighting?

Not necessarily. A gauge is a freedom in how a solution is represented: multiple parameter descriptions may correspond to an equivalent interpretation under a transformation. Normalizing a gauge makes those descriptions more comparable. That is different from claiming that the images contain enough information to resolve every physical ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and illumination. The proposal includes gauge normalization, but does not specify a particular gauge convention or claim that normalization eliminates all uncertainty.
So it would be misleading to say that gauge normalization establishes the true mesh?

Yes. It can fix a convention for describing candidate solutions; it cannot, by that fact alone, establish which geometry the images uniquely support. The posterior is still relevant precisely because uncertainty can remain after a representation has been normalized.
What role do the diffusion priors play? Are they another source of observations?

They are priors, not additional images or known illumination. Conceptually, they provide learned or modeled structure that can favor some candidate configurations over others when the three images leave matters underdetermined. Their presence does not turn a prior preference into direct evidence from the images, nor does the proposal specify their architecture, training data, or the exact variables to which they are applied.
Could a strong prior make the posterior look more decisive even when the images remain ambiguous?

In general, yes: a posterior reflects both image evidence and its priors. If the evidence does not distinguish certain explanations well, prior preferences can have substantial influence. That is worth keeping distinct from a claim that shape, reflectance, and lighting have been identified by the three images alone. The proposal says to use diffusion priors; it does not state how strong their influence will be or what uncertainty will remain.
Where does the LPIPS medoid enter? Is it what gets fitted to the images?

The proposed order is to fit the posterior and then select LPIPS-medoid relightings. A medoid is a representative member of a set, chosen for centrality under a specified dissimilarity. Here LPIPS supplies that perceptual dissimilarity for relightings. That selection is a way to choose an output from possible relightings, not a replacement for fitting the mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior.
Would an LPIPS-medoid relighting be an average of the rendered images?

No. A medoid is selected from the candidate outputs, whereas an average can be a new composite that is not itself one of them. The distinction matters when candidate relightings reflect different plausible joint explanations. The proposal specifies LPIPS-medoid selection but not the number of candidates or an exact selection procedure beyond that characterization.
Does selecting a medoid mean we stop representing uncertainty and output only one answer?

It need not mean that. The medoid supplies a representative relighting for a point-output use, while the fitted posterior is the proposed representation of uncertainty and the calibrated intervals address uncertainty in predicted intensities. Selecting a representative image does not make the other plausible explanations vanish, and the proposal does not say to discard them.
Why choose centrality in LPIPS rather than claim that the selected relighting is physically the most likely one?

They are different claims. LPIPS-medoid selection identifies a relighting that is representative under perceptual distance among the candidates being considered. It does not, solely by being a medoid, establish which mesh, BRDF, or lighting configuration has the greatest posterior probability or is physically correct. The proposal uses LPIPS for selection; it does not equate perceptual centrality with physical certainty.
Would the medoid automatically meet the target of reducing held-out relighting LPIPS by 15% against the matched point-estimate inverse renderer?

No. LPIPS-based selection is aligned with the kind of perceptual comparison in that target, but alignment is not a measured improvement. The requirement remains a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. The proposal supplies a possible way to select relightings; whether it achieves that reduction would have to be evaluated.
Now the interval part: what exactly is conformal calibration intended to change?

It is intended to calibrate predictive intervals for relighting intensities so their observed coverage is closer to the stated nominal level under appropriate evaluation conditions. The target here is 85–95% observed coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. Calibration concerns the intervals’ coverage; it does not by itself change an LPIPS-medoid relighting into a more accurate image.
Does that mean a posterior-derived 90% interval is already guaranteed to cover 90% of held-out intensities?

No. A nominal level is a stated predictive level, not an observed result. Conformal calibration is included precisely as a way to adjust intervals using calibration information rather than simply assuming nominal and observed coverage agree. The proposal does not specify the calibration data, conformity score, or any achieved coverage.
Can we say conformal calibration guarantees that every pixel or every lighting condition gets 90% coverage?

Not from this proposal. Conformal methods have guarantees only under their applicable assumptions and for the particular coverage claim their design supports. The stated requirement is 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities; it does not add a per-pixel, per-condition, or universal 90% guarantee. We should not infer one from the word “conformal.”
Are the uncertainty represented by the posterior and the uncertainty expressed by the intensity intervals the same thing?

They are related but not identical. The posterior concerns possible mesh, BRDF, and lighting configurations. Predictive intensity intervals concern values that may appear in held-out relightings. Predictions can reflect uncertainty carried from the joint reconstruction, while calibration addresses how those intervals cover evaluated intensities. A well-covered intensity interval does not, on its own, prove that uncertainty about each underlying physical component has been perfectly characterized.
Could interval calibration compensate for a poor representative relighting?

It should not be treated as a substitute for relighting quality. Intervals might address uncertainty around predicted intensities, while the LPIPS target evaluates held-out relighting against the matched point-estimate inverse renderer. Both requirements remain distinct: a calibrated interval is not evidence of a 15% LPIPS reduction, and a good LPIPS result is not evidence of 85–95% interval coverage.

If I describe the proposal in one sentence, is this fair: use a normalized joint uncertainty model for geometry, material reflectance, and unknown lighting; choose representative relightings by LPIPS; then calibrate their intensity predictions?

That is broadly faithful. To preserve the specific proposal, I would name a gauge-normalized mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior with diffusion priors, LPIPS-medoid relightings, and conformally calibrated intensity intervals. Those details distinguish the proposed representation, selection rule, and calibration step, while leaving their implementation and measured performance open.
And the reason to keep it joint is that one component might trade off against another when explaining the three images?

Exactly. A joint posterior is meant to retain possible dependencies among mesh, BRDF, and lighting, rather than describing each as though it were known independently. That fits the goal of quantifying ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and lighting under unknown illumination. It does not assert what those dependencies will look like for the three images.
I don't want the proposal to sound like an experimental finding. What's the safest way to state its status?

State it as a method to try: fit the gauge-normalized mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior with diffusion priors, select LPIPS-medoid relightings, and conformally calibrate intensity intervals. Then keep the intended evaluations separate from the proposal itself: the held-out relighting LPIPS reduction of 15% relative to a matched point-estimate inverse renderer and the 85–95% coverage target for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities are requirements, not reported outcomes.
Does gauge normalization preserve shape–lighting ambiguity sufficiently for calibrated intensity intervals under unseen directional lights?

That remains an open question, not something gauge normalization guarantees. Normalization can remove redundant ways of describing the same scene, but it must not erase physically distinct shape–lighting explanations that predict different intensities under an unseen directional light. Whether the resulting intervals are calibrated under those lights depends both on what uncertainty the posterior retains and on whether the calibration applies to those predictions.
What is the distinction between removing a gauge freedom and removing the ambiguity I care about?

A gauge freedom concerns alternative parameter descriptions that represent the same physical prediction once their conventions are handled consistently. Shape–lighting ambiguity concerns alternative explanations of the three images that may make different predictions when the illumination changes. Removing the first can make a posterior easier to interpret. Removing the second without justification could make the posterior, and therefore its predictive intensity intervals, too certain.
So normalization should identify equivalent descriptions, but not force genuinely different explanations to agree?

Exactly. A useful way to phrase the requirement is that normalization should preserve the distinctions relevant to relighting. If two descriptions differ only by a coordinate convention, that difference need not contribute to predictive uncertainty. If they fit the observed images similarly but yield different intensities under a directional light, their difference is relevant to the question and should not disappear merely because a gauge has been fixed.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming a particular normalization scheme?

Consider a change of coordinate frame. Describing the same scene in the new frame need not change its rendered appearance if the geometry and the direction of the light are transformed consistently. That is the sort of representational difference normalization may handle. By contrast, two different surface shapes paired with different explanations of the input lighting might fit the three images but respond differently to a new light direction. Those are potentially distinct predictive explanations, not just two coordinate descriptions.
Why do unseen directional lights make this especially important?

A directional light probes the scene from a specified direction. Shape affects how surfaces are oriented relative to that direction, so alternative shape–lighting explanations that look similar in the input images can diverge when the direction changes. “Unseen” matters because the intervals are being asked to describe intensities beyond the lighting directly represented in those images. This explains why preserving predictive ambiguity matters; it does not establish how large that ambiguity is for the particular three images.
Would preserving multiple mesh and lighting possibilities in the posterior settle the question?

Not by itself. The relevant issue is whether the possibilities retained after gauge normalization include the differences that affect intensities under the unseen directional lights, with uncertainty that carries through to those predictions. A posterior can contain many alternatives yet omit an important ambiguity, or assign it too little weight. Nor does retaining alternatives alone guarantee that the resulting intensity intervals have the desired coverage.
Then what would “preserve ambiguity sufficiently” mean in terms of the intervals?

It means, at minimum, not collapsing distinctions that materially affect the predictive distribution of relighting intensities. If such distinctions are lost, an interval derived from that distribution may be too narrow or misplaced for an unseen directional light. Sufficiency ultimately concerns the intervals’ performance for those predictions, not just whether the normalized parameters appear varied. The question does not state that this sufficiency has been demonstrated.
Could the intervals still look calibrated even if the physical explanation of shape and lighting is wrong?

Yes, intensity coverage and identification of physical components are different claims. Intervals might cover the evaluated intensities without accurately resolving which shape and lighting explanation produced the input images. Conversely, a plausible physical reconstruction does not automatically yield calibrated intervals. The question asks whether gauge normalization retains enough of the relevant ambiguity for intensity prediction; it should not be read as asking whether calibration proves a uniquely correct mesh or light.
Does conformal calibration make up for shape–lighting alternatives that normalization removed?

It should not be assumed to. Conformal calibration can adjust intervals according to the information available to the calibration procedure, but it does not restore missing physical explanations to the mesh–BRDF–lighting posterior. Whether adjusted intervals cover intensities under unseen directional lights also depends on the conditions under which calibration and evaluation are related. The word “conformal” alone does not resolve that question.
Is the concern that calibration could work for some relightings but not for unseen directional ones?

That is a valid concern to articulate, without asserting it happens here. Coverage established for one collection of predictions does not automatically extend to a different lighting setting. If unseen directional lights elicit effects that were not represented adequately in the posterior or in the circumstances relevant to calibration, the intervals could behave differently. The current question is asking whether that gap exists, not reporting one.
How does a direction get interpreted after gauge normalization?

It must be interpreted consistently with the normalized representation. For example, if normalization changes a coordinate convention, the description of a directional light used for relighting must be expressed in the corresponding convention. Otherwise, a changed rendering could result from inconsistent coordinates rather than a meaningful change in shape–lighting uncertainty. No particular coordinate convention or normalization rule is specified here.
Is that coordinate-consistency issue the same as keeping ambiguity in the posterior?

No. Coordinate consistency ensures a light direction and scene description refer to the same physical arrangement when predictions are made. Preserving ambiguity means retaining distinct plausible arrangements when the three images do not distinguish them and when those arrangements can lead to different predictions. Both matter for interpreting intervals under unseen directional lights, but fixing one does not establish the other.
Would it be fair to say that gauge normalization is harmless if it leaves every possible relighting intensity unchanged?

As a conceptual criterion, preserving the predictive intensities associated with equivalent descriptions is important. More precisely, for the uncertainty question, normalization should preserve the distribution of predicted intensities under the directional lights of interest, not merely one chosen rendering. That is a criterion for reasoning about the proposal, not a statement that the proposed normalization has already been shown to satisfy it.
Why emphasize the distribution rather than an LPIPS-medoid relighting?

A medoid is a representative output; it cannot show by itself how widely plausible intensity predictions vary. The intervals depend on predictive uncertainty and their calibration, so the question about preserved ambiguity is about what happens to the range and weighting of predictions after normalization. A representative relighting and a calibrated intensity interval serve different purposes.
Can an interval be too narrow specifically because shape and input lighting traded off in ways the model did not retain?

Conceptually, yes. If distinct shape–lighting explanations fit the three images but would yield different intensities under an unseen directional light, retaining only one explanation could understate predictive uncertainty. That is a possible failure mode, not a finding about the proposed posterior. Interval calibration might affect the reported widths, but its success under those lights still cannot be inferred from the existence of calibration alone.
What if normalization leaves the alternatives in place but changes how much posterior weight each one receives?

That also matters. Predictive intervals depend not only on which explanations remain possible, but on how their predictions contribute to the predictive distribution. A mere change of representation should be handled in a way that does not inadvertently change the intended predictive probabilities. The question does not provide enough detail about the normalization or posterior fitting to determine whether that happens.
So can we answer the original question yes or no now?

Not from the stated proposal alone. We can specify what a satisfactory answer would need to distinguish: redundant parameter descriptions may be normalized away, while physically distinct shape–lighting explanations relevant to unseen directional relighting must remain reflected in predictive intensities. Whether that preservation is sufficient for calibrated intervals under unseen directional lights is an empirical and modeling question, not a guaranteed consequence of gauge normalization.

Here is a hypothesis for the gauge-normalization question: energy normalization with free exposure preserves shape–lighting modes, yielding 85–95% coverage for 90% intervals under unseen directional lights. How should I state that without making it sound established?

State it as a prediction, not a result: “We hypothesize that energy normalization with free exposure preserves the relevant shape–lighting modes and, as a result, yields 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals under unseen directional lights.” That retains both parts of the claim—the preservation of ambiguity and the proposed coverage outcome—without asserting that either has been observed.
What does “energy normalization with free exposure” contribute to the hypothesis?

It names a particular way of handling scale in the lighting-and-image description: energy is normalized while exposure remains free. The hypothesis is that this combination fixes a representational freedom without forcing the shape–lighting explanations that matter for relighting into a single mode. The statement does not specify the normalization formula or how exposure is parameterized, so those details should remain open.
Why mention free exposure explicitly rather than just say “energy normalization”?

Because the hypothesis is about the combination. Normalizing energy establishes a convention, while allowing exposure to remain free leaves room for image brightness to be accounted for without requiring every brightness difference to be assigned to the normalized lighting energy. That explains the proposed role of free exposure; it does not prove that the combination preserves all relevant ambiguity.
Does “shape–lighting modes” mean noise around one reconstruction?

Not necessarily. “Modes” points to distinguishable concentrations of plausible explanations involving shape and lighting, rather than merely small variation around a single explanation. Under the hypothesis, energy normalization with free exposure would retain those distinct explanations when they matter for predicted intensities under unseen directional lights. The hypothesis does not say how many modes there are or describe their particular shapes.
Am I claiming that the shape and lighting can be recovered separately from the three images?

No. The claim goes in a different direction: it predicts that the normalization preserves shape–lighting ambiguity rather than artificially removing it. Preserving modes means keeping plausible alternatives available for prediction, not asserting that the three images uniquely identify shape and lighting.
Could I say that free exposure solves the shape–lighting ambiguity?

That would overstate it. Free exposure is part of the proposed normalization arrangement, but the hypothesis says it helps preserve shape–lighting modes. It does not say exposure resolves those modes, proves which one is physically correct, or removes the underlying ambiguity.
How is this more specific than the earlier question about gauge normalization in general?

It proposes a particular candidate—energy normalization with free exposure—and a particular predicted consequence: preservation of shape–lighting modes together with 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% intervals under unseen directional lights. A question about gauge normalization in general does not, by itself, specify that normalization choice or predict that coverage outcome.
Is the coverage range an uncertainty range around a measured coverage estimate?

No. In this hypothesis, 85–95% is the predicted acceptable observed coverage range for intervals whose nominal level is 90%. It is not a reported measurement and not, by itself, a confidence interval for an estimated coverage percentage.
And the intervals are over relighting intensities, not over the mesh coordinates?

Yes. The associated goal concerns nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. Here the hypothesis focuses that coverage prediction on unseen directional lights. It does not claim 85–95% coverage for intervals over mesh coordinates, lighting parameters, or individual shape–lighting modes.
Why should preserving modes matter for intensity intervals under those lights?

If different plausible shape–lighting explanations predict different intensities when illuminated from an unseen direction, retaining those explanations gives the intensity prediction a chance to reflect that variation. The hypothesis proposes that energy normalization with free exposure retains the relevant modes and thereby supports the stated interval coverage. That is the proposed connection, not evidence yet that the resulting intervals are calibrated.
Would the hypothesis be satisfied just because the posterior displays several modes?

Not necessarily. The claimed modes need to preserve the shape–lighting differences relevant to predictions under unseen directional lights, and the resulting 90% intervals need observed coverage in the stated 85–95% range. Merely displaying more than one mode would not, by itself, establish the coverage part of the hypothesis.
Likewise, if the intervals had the right coverage, would that prove the modes were preserved?

Coverage alone would not identify why it occurred or prove that each relevant shape–lighting mode was retained. The hypothesis contains both a proposed mechanism—mode preservation with energy normalization and free exposure—and a proposed predictive outcome. They are related claims, but an observation about one should not automatically be treated as direct proof of the other.
Could an LPIPS-medoid relighting stand in for checking these modes?

No. An LPIPS medoid selects a representative relighting; it does not show whether distinct shape–lighting explanations remain in the posterior or how their intensity predictions vary. This hypothesis concerns preservation of those explanations and coverage of predictive intensity intervals under unseen directional lights, not just the appearance of one selected relighting.
Does the hypothesis specify a particular directional-light angle or a particular set of unseen lights?

It does not. “Under unseen directional lights” is the stated condition, but no individual directions, number of lights, or evaluation set are given. Adding any of those as though they were part of the hypothesis would introduce details not supplied here.
Should I say energy normalization guarantees coverage because exposure is free?

No. The wording “yielding 85–95% coverage” belongs to a hypothesis, so it is a predicted outcome rather than a guarantee. Free exposure does not, by itself, establish that the posterior retains every relevant mode or that nominal 90% intervals achieve the predicted observed coverage under unseen directional lights.
What remains uncertain in the hypothesis itself?

Both the proposed preservation and its consequence remain uncertain. It is not yet established that energy normalization with free exposure retains the shape–lighting modes that matter for unseen directional relighting, nor that the resulting nominal 90% intensity intervals attain 85–95% coverage under those lights. The hypothesis specifies what is expected, not what has been demonstrated.

Let me try a final phrasing: “With energy normalization but free exposure, distinct shape–lighting explanations should remain available, and 90% intensity intervals should cover 85–95% of held-out intensities under unseen directional lights.” Is that faithful?

Yes, as a statement of the hypothesis. For maximum precision, call the intervals “nominal 90% predictive intervals” and keep “should” so that 85–95% coverage is unmistakably a prediction, not a reported result. The key proposed relationship is that energy normalization with free exposure preserves shape–lighting modes sufficiently to support that coverage under unseen directional lights.

To address whether gauge normalization preserves shape–lighting ambiguity sufficiently for calibrated intensity intervals, I plan to use TriLight-Objects: compare free versus fixed exposure using three-image posteriors, and measure directional-relighting coverage and shape–light correlations. What does that plan actually test?

It sets up a comparison between two exposure treatments, both considered through posteriors fitted from three images. Directional-relighting coverage asks how often predicted intensity intervals contain the corresponding relighting intensities. Shape–light correlations ask how geometry and lighting vary together within the inferred uncertainty. Taken together, those measurements can inform the question of whether the exposure treatment retains shape–lighting ambiguity that matters for relighting. This is a plan; it does not report either measurement or a conclusion.
Why compare free exposure with fixed exposure rather than look only at the free-exposure posterior?

The comparison gives the coverage and correlation measurements a contrast. “Free” allows exposure to vary in the inference, whereas “fixed” does not allow that same freedom. Looking at both may help reveal whether the exposure choice is associated with different predictive coverage or different apparent shape–light dependence. The plan does not predict which condition will have better coverage or stronger correlations.
Does fixed exposure mean that lighting is fixed too?

No. Exposure and lighting are related to image brightness, but they are not interchangeable terms. The comparison specified here is free versus fixed exposure; it does not say that lighting is fixed in the fixed-exposure condition. The plan also does not give the fixed exposure value or describe how lighting is parameterized.
And does free exposure mean every aspect of the reconstruction is left unconstrained?

No. It means exposure is free in the relevant comparison, not that the mesh, reflectance, lighting, or posterior have no constraints. The plan gives no detailed fitting specification beyond using three-image posteriors, so it would be misleading to infer that everything else is unconstrained.
What does “using three-image posteriors” add to the comparison?

It keeps the inference setting tied to the reconstruction problem: the posteriors are based on three images, rather than being descriptions of a scene inferred from an unspecified amount of imagery. It also makes this a comparison of inferred uncertainty, not just two individual reconstructions. The plan does not specify how the three images are selected or whether the two exposure conditions use any particular fitting procedure.
Does naming TriLight-Objects tell us anything about the number of objects or the exact lights?

Not from this plan alone. TriLight-Objects is the named setting for the comparison, but the statement does not give a sample count, light directions, image properties, or a dataset protocol. Those details should not be read into the name.
What should I mean by directional-relighting coverage here?

At the conceptual level, it is the observed fraction of directional-relighting intensity values that fall inside their corresponding predictive intervals. That connects to the goal of 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. The plan says to measure directional-relighting coverage, but does not specify the light directions, the evaluation split, or how coverage is aggregated.
So I shouldn't state that this plan already achieved the 85–95% band?

Correct. The 85–95% band is a target for nominal 90% predictive intervals, not an outcome reported by this plan. Measuring coverage will provide evidence about it once results exist; simply planning the comparison provides none.
Why measure shape–light correlations as well as coverage?

Coverage concerns the intensity predictions. Shape–light correlations concern the relationship among inferred explanations: whether changes in shape tend to accompany changes in lighting within the posterior. Those are complementary views. Coverage alone does not show how the posterior represents shape–lighting ambiguity, while a correlation measurement alone does not show whether predictive intervals cover relighting intensities.
Would a high shape–light correlation demonstrate that the ambiguity was preserved?

Not by itself. A correlation can indicate dependence between quantities as represented by a posterior, but its meaning depends on which quantities are measured and how. It may also fail to capture more complicated relationships or distinct modes. The plan calls for measuring shape–light correlations; it does not specify a numerical threshold that would establish adequate preservation.
Could a low correlation still coexist with meaningful shape–lighting ambiguity?

Yes, conceptually. A single correlation summarizes one kind of association; it need not capture every way that alternative shapes and lights can jointly explain images. That is why it is safer to treat the planned correlations as evidence to interpret alongside directional-relighting coverage, not as a complete measure of ambiguity.
If one condition has better interval coverage, would that automatically tell us its shape–lighting representation is more faithful?

No. Better coverage would speak directly to the intervals in the evaluated directional-relighting setting. It would not, alone, prove that the underlying shape and lighting explanations are physically faithful or that all relevant ambiguity has been retained. The correlations offer another view, but even the two measurements together require careful interpretation rather than an automatic physical conclusion.
Is the free-versus-fixed comparison the same as the goal's comparison against a matched point-estimate inverse renderer?

No. Free versus fixed exposure compares exposure treatments using three-image posteriors. The separate goal asks for a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. This plan names directional-relighting coverage and shape–light correlations as measurements; it does not say that the fixed-exposure condition is that point-estimate baseline or that this comparison measures LPIPS.
Could I infer a difference in relighting LPIPS from a difference in directional-relighting coverage?

Not reliably. Coverage measures how often intensities fall within predictive intervals. LPIPS measures a perceptual difference between relighting images in the specified comparison. A change in one does not, without measurement, establish a change in the other. The plan is focused on coverage and shape–light correlations.
How does this plan connect to the question about unseen directional lights?

The question asks whether shape–lighting ambiguity remains sufficient for calibrated intensity intervals under unseen directional lights. I propose fitting a shadow-aware neural SDF mixture with coupled BRDF–lighting modes, using perceptual-risk relighting and shadow-stratified intensity calibration. Can we unpack what this proposes for reconstructing from three images under unknown illumination?

It proposes four connected elements. A neural signed-distance-field, or SDF, mixture represents alternative geometric explanations with attention to shadows. Coupled BRDF–lighting modes retain plausible reflectance-and-illumination explanations together. Perceptual-risk relighting provides a way to choose or assess relighting outputs with perceptual error in mind. Shadow-stratified intensity calibration addresses predictive intervals for intensities in shadow and lit regions. Together, these are intended to support relightable geometry and materials while expressing ambiguity; they are not reported results.
What does an SDF contribute to the geometry side?

An SDF is a way to represent a surface through a function whose zero level set defines the surface. A neural SDF uses a neural representation for that function. Here it is the proposed geometric representation, but the proposal does not specify its architecture, how surfaces are extracted, or how its parameters are fitted.

A mixture can represent more than one plausible geometric explanation instead of requiring all uncertainty to be expressed around one surface description. That fits the goal of quantifying ambiguity from only three images. The proposal does not say how many mixture components there are, how they are weighted, or whether they correspond to any particular shapes.

No. It is a proposed capacity to represent alternatives, not an observation about the images or a result of fitting them. Whether distinct geometric explanations appear, and how much they affect relighting, would depend on the fitted model and evidence.

It means the proposed representation or fitting should account for shadows as part of explaining and predicting image appearance. Shadows can be relevant to geometry and illumination, so treating them explicitly is pertinent to relighting. The phrase alone does not specify a shadow model, a visibility algorithm, a labeling method, or any achieved improvement in shadow prediction.

No. The proposal mentions shadows in two distinct places. “Shadow-aware neural SDF mixture” qualifies the geometric approach, while “shadow-stratified intensity calibration” qualifies how predictive intensities are calibrated. Those roles may relate, but the wording does not make the shadow-aware representation merely a pixel classifier or say they use the same implementation.

It should not be presented as a guarantee of that. Shadows can provide information about scene structure and lighting, but illumination is unknown, and different explanations may remain plausible. The mixture and coupled modes are proposed precisely in a setting where ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and lighting matters.
What does BRDF stand for in the coupled modes?

It stands for bidirectional reflectance distribution function, a description of how a surface reflects light as illumination and viewing directions vary. In the proposal, BRDF is the reflectance side of the material-and-lighting explanation. No particular BRDF parameterization or material class is specified.
Why couple BRDF and lighting instead of treating their uncertainties independently?

Because a material and an illumination explanation can work together to account for appearance. Keeping BRDF–lighting modes coupled allows the model to represent plausible combinations rather than freely recombining each reflectance possibility with every lighting possibility. That is the proposed representational idea; the proposal does not give the modes, their number, or a claim that they have been recovered accurately.

Both serve the larger purpose of representing plausible explanations for the images and their relightings: the neural SDF mixture concerns geometric alternatives, and the coupled modes concern reflectance and lighting alternatives.
